os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three requirements for a correct critical-section solution?
options: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting
All processes must run at the same speed
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: A solution must provide mutual exclusion, progress (no indefinite blocking when the section is free) and bounded waiting, while making no assumptions about relative speeds. Requiring equal speeds is exactly the assumption a correct solution must avoid.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: Two threads each run `counter++` 1,000 times on a shared variable with no locking. The final value is 1,873. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The CPU dropped some instructions under load
`counter++` is a load, add and store; interleaved updates overwrote each other
One thread was starved and ran only 873 times
Integer overflow wrapped the value
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: Both threads can load the same old value, add 1 and store it, losing one increment. This race condition can produce any value below 2,000. The threads did run all their iterations; the updates were simply lost.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: In Peterson's solution, process i runs `flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j) {}`. If both processes set their flags at nearly the same time, who enters first?
options: The process whose write to `turn` happened first
The process with the lower index, always
The process whose write to `turn` happened last waits; the other enters
Both enter, and mutual exclusion is restored on exit
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: Each process politely sets `turn` to the other. The last writer's value sticks, so it is the one that yields and spins while the other enters. Writing first means your value gets overwritten, which lets you in rather than making you wait.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: A developer reorders Peterson's entry code to `turn = j; flag[i] = true; while (flag[j] && turn == j) {}`. What breaks?
options: Mutual exclusion: both processes can end up in the critical section together
Nothing; the order of the two writes doesn't matter
Only bounded waiting; mutual exclusion still holds
The code deadlocks every time both processes try to enter
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: P0 sets turn = 1, P1 sets turn = 0, P1 sets flag[1] and sees flag[0] false, so it enters. P0 then sets flag[0], sees turn == 0 (not 1) and also enters. Announcing interest must come before yielding the turn.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: Why can Peterson's algorithm fail on modern multicore CPUs even when the code looks correct?
options: Modern CPUs don't support busy waiting
Compilers refuse to compile spin loops
It only fails on single-core CPUs
CPUs and compilers may reorder a store and a later load, so a process can read the other's flag before its own write is visible
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: Peterson assumes sequential consistency. Store buffers (even on x86, which allows store-load reordering) and compiler optimizations can let both processes read the other's flag as false. Memory fences or atomic operations with sequentially consistent ordering are needed.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: A two-process lock uses only a shared `turn` variable: process i waits while `turn != i`, then sets `turn = j` on exit. Which requirement does it violate?
options: Mutual exclusion
Progress: a process can be blocked even when the critical section is free, if the other doesn't want to enter
Bounded waiting
It satisfies all three requirements
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: Strict alternation forces turns: if P1 never wants to enter again, P0 cannot enter a second time because turn stays at 1. Mutual exclusion holds, which is why it looks plausible, but progress fails.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: Disabling interrupts around a critical section is a valid technique in which situation?
options: Inside a kernel on a single-processor system, for very short sections
In user-space code on any system
On multiprocessor systems, because it stops all CPUs
For long critical sections that do disk I/O
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: On a uniprocessor, no other code can run if interrupts are off, so short kernel sections are safe. It's a privileged operation (not available to user code), doesn't stop other CPUs on a multiprocessor, and holding it during long operations would lose interrupts and hurt responsiveness.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: Assuming sequentially consistent memory, which properties does Peterson's two-process solution guarantee? Select all that apply.
options: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting
Correctness for any number of processes as written
No busy waiting
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: Peterson's solution meets all three critical-section requirements for two processes. It is defined for exactly two (generalizations like the filter algorithm exist), and it spins in a while loop, so it does busy-wait.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: Which approaches make a shared counter increment safe across threads? Select all that apply.
options: An atomic fetch-and-add instruction
Protecting the increment with a mutex
Declaring the variable `volatile` in C/C++
`Atomics.add` on an Int32Array backed by a SharedArrayBuffer in JavaScript worker threads
Adding a random sleep before each increment
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: Atomic read-modify-write instructions (including JS `Atomics.add`) and mutexes make the increment indivisible. In C/C++, `volatile` only prevents some compiler optimizations; it does not make `++` atomic. Random sleeps only change how often the race shows up.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: Peterson's solution, written with plain loads and stores, guarantees mutual exclusion on x86 multicore CPUs without any memory fences.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: False. x86 allows a store to be delayed in the store buffer while a later load to a different address proceeds, which is exactly the store-then-load pattern Peterson depends on. A full fence (e.g., MFENCE) or a locked instruction is required.

os-sync-deadlock:0.prompt: Single-threaded Node.js code can still have race conditions, for example when two async handlers read a value, `await` something, then write back a modified value.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:0.explanation: True. JavaScript never runs two pieces of code at once, but an `await` lets other handlers run between the read and the write, so a read-modify-write that spans an `await` can lose updates. The lost update is the same kind as with threads; only the interleaving points differ.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: In the classic bounded-buffer (producer-consumer) solution with a buffer of N slots, how are the three semaphores initialized?
options: mutex = 0, empty = 0, full = N
mutex = 1, empty = 1, full = 1
mutex = 1, empty = N, full = 0
mutex = N, empty = N, full = N
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: mutex = 1 gives mutual exclusion on the buffer, empty = N counts free slots (all free initially) and full = 0 counts filled slots (none yet). Starting full at N would let consumers read items that don't exist.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: What is the key conceptual difference between a mutex and a counting semaphore?
options: A mutex has an owner and must be released by the thread that locked it; a semaphore is a counter that any thread may signal
A semaphore can only take values 0 and 1
A mutex can be used across processes but a semaphore cannot
A semaphore never blocks a thread
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: A mutex models ownership of a lock (enabling error checking, recursion and priority inheritance). A semaphore is just a counter with atomic wait/signal, so one thread can wait and a different one signal, which is what makes it useful for signaling. Values limited to 0 and 1 describe a binary semaphore.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: A producer is written as below while the consumer uses the textbook order. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; the order of wait calls never matters
Items may be consumed twice
The buffer may overflow by one item
Deadlock: when the buffer is full, the producer sleeps holding mutex, so the consumer can never enter to free a slot
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: The producer blocks on empty while holding mutex; the consumer then blocks on mutex and can never signal empty. Always wait on the counting semaphore before acquiring the mutex. Overflow can't happen because wait(empty) still guards the slot.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: A Node.js service must allow at most 10 concurrent outbound calls to a rate-limited API. Which primitive models this most directly?
options: A mutex
A counting semaphore initialized to 10
A condition variable with no state
A binary semaphore initialized to 0
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: Each call acquires a permit (wait) and releases it when done (signal); the 11th caller waits until a permit is free. A mutex would allow only one call at a time. Libraries like p-limit implement this async semaphore pattern.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: Statement S2 in thread B must run only after statement S1 in thread A. Using a semaphore `s`, A does `S1; signal(s);` and B does `wait(s); S2;`. What must `s` be initialized to?
options: It doesn't matter
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: Starting at 0 makes B block until A signals after S1. Starting at 1 would let B pass immediately and run S2 before S1. This ordering use is why semaphores, unlike mutexes, may be signaled by a thread that never waited.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: A low-priority task holds a lock needed by a high-priority task, and a medium-priority task keeps preempting the low one, so the high-priority task misses deadlines. Which fix addresses this, and which primitive supports it?
options: Use a counting semaphore so the high task can proceed without the lock
Disable the scheduler while any lock is held
Priority inheritance, which needs a lock with a known owner such as a mutex
Raise the medium task's priority above the high task's
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: This is priority inversion (famously hit by Mars Pathfinder). Priority inheritance temporarily boosts the lock holder to the waiter's priority so the medium task can't preempt it. That requires knowing who holds the lock, which a mutex tracks and a plain semaphore doesn't.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: In a bounded buffer with several producers, the `empty` and `full` semaphores already ensure there's a free slot. Why is the `mutex` still needed?
options: To make `empty` and `full` atomic
Two producers can pass wait(empty) together and both write to the same `buffer[in]` before `in` is advanced
To stop consumers from reading when the buffer is empty
It isn't needed with multiple producers, only with multiple consumers
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: The counting semaphores guarantee capacity, not exclusive access to the shared index. Without the mutex, the read-update of `in` races and items overwrite each other. Stopping consumers on an empty buffer is the job of `full`, not the mutex.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: Which statements about semaphores are correct? Select all that apply.
options: wait and signal must each execute atomically
In some implementations a negative value equals the number of blocked waiters
A binary semaphore initialized to 1 can provide mutual exclusion
Only the thread that called wait may call signal
Using semaphores rules out deadlock
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: Atomic wait/signal is the defining property; textbook implementations let the value go negative to count waiters, and a binary semaphore at 1 works as a lock. There's no ownership rule (that's a mutex), and misordered waits easily deadlock.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: Which are appropriate uses of a counting semaphore? Select all that apply.
options: Limiting concurrent use of a pool of N identical resources
Counting the filled slots in a bounded buffer
Making one thread wait for another's event, with the semaphore starting at 0
Ensuring only the acquiring thread can release the lock
Letting the same thread re-acquire a lock it already holds
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: Semaphores excel at counting resources and signaling events. Owner-only release and recursive acquisition both require ownership tracking, which mutexes (e.g., recursive mutexes) provide and semaphores don't.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: In the textbook bounded-buffer solution, the consumer calls wait(full) before wait(mutex).
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: True. The consumer first waits for an item to exist, then locks the buffer. Reversing the order could make it sleep on an empty buffer while holding the mutex, blocking every producer.

os-sync-deadlock:1.prompt: A mutex and a binary semaphore are interchangeable in every respect, including ownership and support for priority inheritance.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:1.explanation: False. Both can give mutual exclusion, but a mutex has an owner, so it can detect misuse, support recursion and implement priority inheritance. A binary semaphore has no owner and can be signaled by any thread.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: What core guarantee does a monitor provide?
options: Only one thread can be active inside the monitor's procedures at a time
Threads inside the monitor never block
Deadlock between monitors is impossible
Every procedure runs on a dedicated CPU
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: A monitor bundles shared data with procedures and an implicit lock so only one thread executes inside at once; condition variables handle waiting. Threads can still block (on condition variables), and two monitors can deadlock if they call each other in opposite orders.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: What does calling wait() on a condition variable do?
options: Spins until the condition becomes true
Atomically releases the associated lock and suspends the thread; the lock is re-acquired before wait returns
Suspends the thread while keeping the lock so no one else changes the state
Checks the condition once and returns immediately
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: Releasing the lock and sleeping must be atomic, otherwise a signal could slip in between and be lost. Keeping the lock while asleep would stop any other thread from making the condition true.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: Why should a condition variable wait be written as `while (!ready) cond.wait(lock)` instead of `if (!ready) cond.wait(lock)`?
options: `while` is faster than `if` in compiled code
`if` would deadlock immediately
Wakeups can be spurious, and under Mesa semantics another thread may change the state before the woken thread runs
The condition variable requires the predicate to be evaluated exactly twice
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: A woken thread just becomes runnable; by the time it re-acquires the lock, another thread may have consumed the item, and POSIX also permits spurious wakeups. Rechecking in a loop makes the code correct either way. `if` doesn't deadlock; it acts on a stale condition.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: A thread calls signal() on a condition variable when no thread is waiting. A moment later another thread calls wait(). What happens?
options: The waiter returns immediately because the earlier signal was remembered
The waiter blocks; the earlier signal had no effect because condition variables have no memory
The program throws an error because signal was called with no waiters
The waiter returns after a fixed timeout
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: Unlike a semaphore, whose signal increments a counter, a condition variable signal with no waiters is lost. That's why the waiter must check a separate predicate under the lock before waiting.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: Java's built-in monitors and POSIX condition variables use Mesa (signal-and-continue) semantics. What does that mean?
options: The signaled thread runs immediately and the signaler waits
Signals are queued and delivered in FIFO order to future waiters
The signaler keeps the lock and continues; the woken thread competes for the lock later and must recheck the condition
Only one condition variable per monitor is allowed
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: In Mesa semantics, signal is a hint: the waiter moves to the ready set and reacquires the lock later, by which time the state may have changed. Hoare semantics hand the lock directly to the waiter, which is option one.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: In Java, producers and consumers all `wait()` on the same object's monitor for different conditions (not full vs not empty). The code uses `notify()` and occasionally all threads end up waiting forever. Why?
options: notify() releases the lock too early
notify() can wake a thread of the wrong kind (a producer instead of a consumer); it rechecks, waits again, and the needed thread is never woken
wait() must be called outside a synchronized block
Java monitors don't support more than two waiting threads
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: With one wait set shared by different conditions, notify() wakes an arbitrary waiter. If it wakes one that can't proceed, the signal is effectively consumed and everyone may sleep. Use notifyAll(), or separate Condition objects from a ReentrantLock.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: A producer sets `ready = true` and calls `pthread_cond_signal` without holding the mutex. The consumer does `lock; while (!ready) cond_wait; unlock`. Occasionally the consumer sleeps forever. What's the race?
options: The producer's update and signal can land after the consumer checks `ready` but before it starts waiting, so the wakeup is lost
pthread_cond_signal always fails without the mutex
The consumer's while loop should be an if
The mutex is released twice
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: Checking the predicate and calling wait are atomic only with respect to threads that also hold the mutex. Because the producer changed `ready` without it, its write and signal can fall into that gap. Modify the predicate under the mutex (signaling while holding it or right after is then fine).

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: Which statements about condition variables are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A condition variable is used together with a mutex or monitor lock
wait() must be called while holding that lock
When wait() returns, the calling thread holds the lock again
broadcast (notifyAll) wakes all waiting threads
A condition variable keeps a count of past signals like a semaphore
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: Condition variables pair with a lock protecting the predicate; wait releases and reacquires it, and broadcast wakes every waiter. They store no signal count, which is why the predicate must be checked explicitly.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: Which statements about monitors in Java are correct? Select all that apply.
options: `synchronized` methods on an object use that object's monitor
Calling wait() without holding the object's monitor throws IllegalMonitorStateException
notify() releases the monitor immediately, before the synchronized block ends
A ReentrantLock can have several Condition objects, e.g., notFull and notEmpty
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: Every Java object has a monitor used by synchronized; wait/notify require owning it; ReentrantLock.newCondition() gives separate wait sets. notify() does not release the lock: the woken thread can only proceed after the notifier leaves the synchronized block.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: In a Mesa-style monitor, a signaled thread runs immediately, before the signaling thread continues.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: False. That describes Hoare semantics. In Mesa semantics the signaler continues holding the lock, and the woken thread runs later after re-acquiring it, so it must re-test its condition.

os-sync-deadlock:2.prompt: Calling signal on a condition variable that has no waiting threads has no lasting effect.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:2.explanation: True. Condition variables are stateless, so the signal is simply lost, unlike a semaphore's signal, which increments its count. Correct code therefore relies on a shared predicate, not on the signal itself.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four necessary (Coffman) conditions for deadlock?
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
Starvation
Circular wait
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Starvation is a separate liveness problem: a thread is postponed indefinitely while others make progress.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: When every resource type has exactly one instance, how is deadlock detected?
options: Find a cycle in the wait-for graph
Run the Banker's safety algorithm on maximum claims
Check whether any process has waited longer than a timeout
Count total held resources against total available
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: With single instances, a cycle in the wait-for graph (process waits on process) is necessary and sufficient for deadlock. The Banker's algorithm is for avoidance, and timeouts only suggest a deadlock without proving one.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: A resource-allocation graph with multiple instances per resource type contains a cycle. What can you conclude?
options: The system is definitely deadlocked
The system is definitely not deadlocked
A deadlock may exist; a cycle is necessary but not sufficient
The graph was drawn incorrectly
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: With several instances, a process outside the cycle may hold an instance and release it, breaking the cycle. So a cycle means deadlock is possible, not certain; a matrix-based detection algorithm is needed to decide.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: Resources A and B; Available = (0, 0). P0 holds (1,0), requests (0,1). P1 holds (0,1), requests (1,0). P2 holds (0,0), requests (0,0). Which processes are deadlocked?
options: P0, P1 and P2
None, because P2 can finish
Only P1
P0 and P1
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: P2 needs nothing, finishes and releases (0,0), so Available stays (0,0). P0 needs B held by P1, and P1 needs A held by P0, so neither can be satisfied. P2 finishing doesn't help because it frees no resources.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: Running deadlock detection on every resource request is accurate but costly. What is a common compromise?
options: Never run detection
Run detection periodically or when CPU utilization drops below a threshold
Run detection only when a process terminates normally
Run detection only at system boot
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: Deadlocked processes stop doing work, so falling utilization or a periodic timer is a cheap trigger. The trade-off: the longer between runs, the more processes may get caught in the deadlock and the harder it is to tell which request caused it.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, transaction T1 updates row A then row B, while T2 updates row B then row A, at the same time. What happens?
options: Both transactions hang forever until an administrator intervenes
Both transactions are rolled back automatically
PostgreSQL silently merges the two updates
After about deadlock_timeout (default 1s), PostgreSQL detects the cycle, aborts one with a 'deadlock detected' error, and the other proceeds
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: PostgreSQL waits deadlock_timeout before running its wait-for graph check, then cancels one transaction so the other can finish. The application should retry the aborted one, and preferably lock rows in a consistent order to avoid the cycle.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: When choosing a victim to terminate or roll back during deadlock recovery, how do you prevent the same process from being picked every time?
options: Always pick the process with the lowest PID
Include the number of times a process has already been rolled back in the cost factor
Always pick the process holding the most resources
Choose a victim uniformly at random each time, ignoring history
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: A pure cost-based choice can keep picking the same cheap process, starving it. Counting previous rollbacks in the cost makes it progressively less likely to be chosen. Random choice lowers the chance of repeats but gives no bound.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: Which are valid ways to recover once a deadlock is detected? Select all that apply.
options: Abort all deadlocked processes
Abort deadlocked processes one at a time until the cycle is broken
Preempt resources from a victim and roll it back to a safe point
Wait, since deadlocks eventually resolve themselves
Raise the priority of all deadlocked processes
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: Recovery means breaking the cycle by termination or preemption with rollback. A deadlock is permanent by definition, and priority changes don't release any resources.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: Which techniques prevent deadlock by negating one of the four necessary conditions? Select all that apply.
options: Acquiring locks in one global order
Requesting all needed resources at once before starting
Using tryLock and releasing held locks if the next one can't be acquired
Adding more worker threads
Making every lock reentrant
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: A global order removes circular wait; all-at-once requests remove hold and wait; tryLock-and-back-off means a thread never waits while holding locks. More threads change nothing, and reentrancy only lets a thread re-take its own lock; it doesn't stop cycles between threads.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: In a resource-allocation graph where every resource type has exactly one instance, any cycle means the processes in it are deadlocked.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: True. With single instances there's no other holder who could release a resource, so each process in the cycle waits forever on the next. With multiple instances, a cycle is only a possibility.

os-sync-deadlock:3.prompt: General-purpose OSes like Linux run a deadlock detection algorithm over user-space mutexes and kill a victim process when they find a cycle.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:3.explanation: False. For application locks they effectively ignore deadlock (the 'ostrich' approach) and leave prevention to the programmer. Detection and recovery are found in systems like databases, which can abort and retry transactions.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: What extra information does the Banker's algorithm require from each process up front?
options: Its expected running time
The maximum number of instances of each resource type it may ever need
The exact order in which it will request resources
Its scheduling priority
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: Banker's avoids deadlock by ensuring the system can always satisfy every process's declared maximum in some order. It doesn't need request order or running time, only maximum claims.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: In the Banker's algorithm, what does it mean for a state to be 'safe'?
options: No process is currently waiting
All resources are currently free
Some order exists in which every process can obtain its maximum need, finish and release its resources
Every process holds at least one resource
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: A state is safe if a safe sequence exists: each process's remaining need can be met with available resources plus those released by earlier processes. Processes may still be waiting in a safe state; what matters is that all can eventually finish.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: Process P0 has Max = (7, 5, 3) and Allocation = (0, 1, 0) for resources A, B, C. What is its Need?
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: Need = Max - Allocation = (7-0, 5-1, 3-0) = (7, 4, 3). Adding instead of subtracting gives (7, 6, 3).

Work (3,3,2): P1 fits, then Work = (5,3,2); P3 fits, (7,4,3); P4 fits, (7,4,5); P2 fits, (10,4,7); P0 fits. P0 and P4 can't go first (need exceeds 3 of A), and after P1, P2 needs 6 of A but only 5 are free.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: Same system after granting P1's request (1,0,2): Available = (2,3,0). P4 now requests (3,3,0). What does the Banker's algorithm do?
options: Grants it, since P4's total need covers it
Grants it only if the resulting state is safe
P4 must wait, because the request exceeds what is currently available
Raises an error because P4 exceeded its maximum claim
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: The checks are request <= Need (3,3,0 <= 4,3,1: fine) and request <= Available (3 > 2 for A: fails). So P4 waits; the safety check isn't even reached. An error is only raised if a request exceeds the process's remaining Need.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: Available = (2,3,0). Needs: P0 (7,4,3), P1 (0,2,0), P2 (6,0,0), P3 (0,1,1), P4 (4,3,1). P0 requests (0,2,0), which is available. Why does the Banker's algorithm refuse it?
options: The request exceeds P0's maximum claim
Granting it leaves Available = (2,1,0), from which no process's need can be met, so the state would be unsafe
P0 already holds too many resources
Requests for resource B are never granted to P0
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: After pretending to grant: Available (2,1,0); P0 need becomes (7,2,3). P1 needs 2 of B (only 1 left), P3 needs 1 of C (0 left), P2 and P4 need more A. No process can finish, so the state is unsafe and P0 must wait even though the resources are free.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: Why is the Banker's algorithm rarely used in general-purpose operating systems?
options: It requires knowing future resource needs in advance, assumes a fixed set of processes and resources, and costs O(m·n²) per request
It can't handle more than one resource type
It allows deadlocks in safe states
It only works with a single CPU
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: Real programs rarely know their maximum needs, processes come and go, and running a safety check on every allocation is expensive. It handles multiple resource types fine, and a safe state can't deadlock as long as processes stay within their declared maximums.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: When a process makes a request, which steps does the Banker's resource-request algorithm perform? Select all that apply.
options: Raise an error if the request exceeds the process's remaining Need
Make the process wait if the request exceeds Available
Tentatively allocate and run the safety algorithm; roll back and make it wait if unsafe
Grant the request whenever it fits in Available, regardless of safety
Compare the request against other processes' Max values
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: The three checks are: within Need, within Available, and safe after allocation. Granting whenever resources are free is exactly what Banker's avoids; other processes' Max matters only through the safety check on their Need.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: Which data structures does the Banker's algorithm maintain for n processes and m resource types? Select all that apply.
options: Available: vector of length m
Max: n x m matrix
Allocation: n x m matrix
Need: n x m matrix (Max - Allocation)
A wait-for graph between processes
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: Banker's works with Available, Max, Allocation and Need. A wait-for graph is used for deadlock detection with single-instance resources, not for avoidance.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: Every unsafe state is a deadlocked state.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: False. Unsafe means the OS can no longer guarantee that deadlock is avoided; processes might release resources early or not request their maximum, so deadlock may never happen. Deadlocked states are a subset of unsafe states.

os-sync-deadlock:4.prompt: The Banker's safety algorithm takes O(m × n²) time for m resource types and n processes.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:4.explanation: True. Each of up to n passes scans n processes and compares m-length vectors. That per-request cost is one reason Banker's is impractical for large, dynamic systems.

options: Threads blocked forever waiting on each other's locks
Threads that keep changing state in response to each other, staying active but making no progress
A thread that is never scheduled because others have higher priority
A lock that is held across a system call
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: Like two people stepping aside in a hallway in the same direction repeatedly, livelocked threads are running and reacting, yet nothing gets done. Blocked forever is deadlock; never scheduled is starvation.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: How does starvation differ from deadlock?
options: Starvation affects only the kernel
Starvation always involves a cycle of waiting processes
In starvation, a process is postponed indefinitely while others keep making progress
They are the same thing
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: In deadlock a set of processes all wait on each other and nobody in the set progresses. In starvation the system works, but one process keeps losing (e.g., to higher priorities). Cycles are a feature of deadlock, not starvation.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: Two threads each lock one resource, tryLock the other, and on failure release and immediately retry. They livelock. What is the standard fix?
options: Retry faster so one thread wins
Replace tryLock with a blocking lock
Remove the release step so each keeps its first lock
Add randomized (often exponential) backoff before retrying
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: Randomized delays break the symmetry so one thread gets both locks first, as in Ethernet's CSMA/CD backoff. Blocking locks or keeping the first lock reintroduce hold-and-wait and risk deadlock; a consistent lock order is the other clean fix.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: Under strict priority scheduling, a low-priority job never runs because high-priority jobs keep arriving. What is the classic fix?
options: Aging: gradually raise the priority of jobs the longer they wait
Lower the priority of the low job further
Use a larger time quantum
Kill the low-priority job
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: Aging ensures any waiting job eventually reaches a high enough priority to run, bounding its wait. A larger quantum doesn't help a job that is never picked in the first place.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: An unfair lock lets a newly arriving thread grab a just-released lock ahead of queued waiters ('barging'). What's the trade-off compared with a fair FIFO (ticket) lock?
options: Unfair locks have lower throughput but prevent starvation
There's no difference under contention
Unfair locks usually give higher throughput but can starve a waiting thread; fair locks bound waiting at a throughput cost
Fair locks can deadlock while unfair locks cannot
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: Barging avoids handing the lock to a sleeping thread that must be woken (a context switch), so throughput improves, but an unlucky thread can lose repeatedly. Java's ReentrantLock is unfair by default and offers a fair mode for this reason.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: A downstream service has a brief outage. Thousands of clients retry every exactly 1 second; when it comes back it is immediately overwhelmed again and stays down. Which fix best addresses this?
options: Retry every 100 ms so requests get through sooner
Exponential backoff with random jitter, plus a cap on retries (or a circuit breaker)
Increase client timeouts to 60 seconds
Make every client retry at the same scheduled time
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: Synchronized retries form a thundering herd: the system is busy but makes no progress, much like livelock. Jitter spreads retries out, backoff reduces load, and circuit breakers stop hammering a failing dependency. Faster or synchronized retries amplify the herd.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: Many workers update the same 'hot' row using optimistic concurrency (read version, compute, UPDATE ... WHERE version = v, retry on mismatch). Throughput collapses and some workers almost never succeed. What's the best remedy?
options: Retry the failed updates immediately in a tight loop
Remove the version check so updates always succeed
Add more workers to increase the chance of success
Reduce contention on that row, e.g., serialize through a queue, use a pessimistic lock, or split the row into shards
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are rare; on a hot row most attempts fail, wasting work and starving unlucky workers. Serializing access, locking, or sharding the counter removes the conflict. Dropping the version check causes lost updates.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: Which of these can cause starvation? Select all that apply.
options: Strict priority scheduling without aging
A reader-preference readers-writers lock under a steady stream of readers
A greedy 'nearest request first' policy such as SSTF disk scheduling
A FIFO queue with bounded service time
Round-robin scheduling with a fixed quantum
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: Priority without aging, reader preference and greedy nearest-first selection all let some requests be bypassed indefinitely. FIFO and round-robin give every waiter a bounded turn.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish livelock from deadlock? Select all that apply.
options: Livelocked threads are running and consuming CPU
Deadlocked threads are blocked and consume little CPU
Neither livelock nor deadlock makes progress on the stuck work
Livelock always resolves itself after a while
A wait-for graph cycle check reliably detects livelock
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: Both make no progress, but livelock burns CPU while deadlock sits idle. Livelock can persist indefinitely without a symmetry breaker, and since livelocked threads aren't waiting on each other's locks, a wait-for graph shows no cycle.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: A livelocked system typically shows high CPU usage even though no useful work completes.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: True. Livelocked threads keep executing retries and state changes. That busy-but-stuck signature is how you tell it apart from deadlock, where the threads are asleep.

os-sync-deadlock:5.prompt: If a lock implementation is deadlock-free, every individual thread is guaranteed to eventually acquire it.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:5.explanation: False. Deadlock-freedom only guarantees that some thread makes progress; a particular thread may lose forever. Starvation-freedom is the stronger property that guarantees every thread eventually succeeds.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: What does a readers-writers lock allow?
options: Exactly one reader or one writer at a time
Many concurrent readers, or exactly one writer with no readers
Many writers concurrently as long as no readers are active
Readers and writers concurrently, as long as they touch different fields
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: Reads don't conflict with each other, so they can run in parallel; a writer needs exclusive access. Allowing readers alongside a writer would expose half-written state.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: In the 'first' readers-writers problem (readers preference), who can starve?
options: Readers
Neither; it is starvation-free
Writers
Both equally
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: New readers can join while any reader is active, so a continuous stream of overlapping readers keeps the writer waiting indefinitely. The 'second' problem (writer preference) flips this and can starve readers.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: In the classic readers-preference solution, why is the `read_count` variable protected by its own mutex, separate from `rw_mutex`?
options: Because readers update read_count concurrently, and the first/last reader decision must be atomic
Because writers need to modify read_count
To make reads faster than writes
To let writers enter while readers are active
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: Each reader increments read_count on entry and decrements on exit; the first reader locks rw_mutex and the last unlocks it. Without a mutex two readers could both think they're first or last. Writers never touch read_count.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: A cache map is read on every request (lookups take about 50 ns) and updated rarely. Replacing its mutex with a reader-writer lock made throughput worse on a 32-core machine. What's the likely reason?
options: Reader-writer locks don't allow concurrent readers
Writers starved the readers
The mutex was already lock-free
With very short critical sections, every reader atomically updating the shared reader count causes cache-line contention that outweighs the parallelism
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: Taking a read lock still writes to shared state (the reader count), so all cores fight over one cache line. RW locks pay off when read sections are long; for tiny ones, RCU, sharded locks or immutable snapshots scale better. Writers are rare here, so starvation isn't the issue.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: In a writer-preference readers-writers lock, what happens to a new reader that arrives while a writer is waiting?
options: It enters immediately if other readers are active
It waits until the waiting writer has finished
It aborts with an error
It is upgraded to a writer
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: To keep writers from starving, new readers are held back once a writer is queued; current readers drain, the writer runs, then readers resume. The trade-off is that a stream of writers can starve readers.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: Two threads each hold a read lock on the same RW lock and both try to upgrade to a write lock without releasing the read lock. What happens?
options: Deadlock: each waits for the other's read lock to be released
One upgrade succeeds automatically
Both become writers at the same time
The read locks are silently released
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: A writer needs all readers gone, and each upgrader is a reader waiting on the other. This is why many RW locks don't allow upgrades (or allow just one 'upgradable' holder); the usual pattern is to release the read lock, take the write lock, and re-check the state.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: In PostgreSQL, transactions T1 and T2 both run `SELECT ... FOR SHARE` on the same row, then T3 runs `UPDATE` on that row. What happens?
options: T2 waits for T1, and T3 proceeds immediately
All three proceed concurrently
T1 and T2 both hold the shared row lock concurrently; T3 waits until both finish
T3 aborts with a serialization error immediately
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: Row-level FOR SHARE locks are compatible with each other (like read locks), so T1 and T2 coexist. UPDATE needs a conflicting lock, so T3 blocks until both shared holders commit or roll back, which is exactly the readers-writers pattern.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: Which statements about reader-writer locks are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Multiple readers can hold the lock at the same time
A writer excludes both readers and other writers
The fairness policy decides whether readers or writers can starve
A reader can always upgrade to a writer safely without releasing its read lock
A reader-writer lock is always faster than a plain mutex
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: Shared reads, exclusive writes, and a policy choice that determines who may starve. Upgrades can deadlock if two readers attempt them, and RW locks carry extra overhead that loses to a mutex for short or write-heavy sections.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: Which techniques are used as alternatives to reader-writer locks for read-mostly data? Select all that apply.
options: Read-copy-update (RCU)
Copy-on-write snapshots published by atomically swapping a pointer
Sequence locks (seqlocks), where readers retry if a write happened during their read
Protecting everything with a single global spinlock
Disabling CPU caches for the shared data
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: RCU, copy-on-write snapshots and seqlocks let readers proceed with little or no shared writes, which scales far better for read-heavy data. A global spinlock serializes readers, and disabling caches would be catastrophically slow.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: In the readers-preference solution, a steady stream of overlapping readers can keep a writer waiting forever.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: True. As long as at least one reader is active, rw_mutex stays held by the reader group and new readers keep joining, so the writer never gets in. Writer-preference or fair (phase-fair) locks address this.

os-sync-deadlock:6.prompt: A reader-writer lock lets a writer proceed while readers are active, as long as the writer modifies different fields from those being read.
options: True
False
os-sync-deadlock:6.explanation: False. The lock knows nothing about which fields are touched; a writer always waits for all readers to leave. Finer-grained concurrency needs finer-grained locks or lock-free structures.
